blocks.prompt: The Axolotl That Never Grew Up
blocks.text: Most tadpoles grow up. They lose their gills. They climb out of the water and hop away as frogs. The axolotl does not do that. The axolotl keeps its feathery gills. It keeps its little tail. It stays in the water its whole life. An axolotl can lose a leg and grow a brand new one. It can do this again and again. Its mouth curves up, so it always looks like it is smiling.

blocks.prompt: The Salamander That Stayed a Baby
blocks.text: Almost every salamander begins life in the water. It hatches with feathery gills and a long tail for swimming. As it grows, its body changes. The gills shrink away, lungs take over, and the grown salamander walks out onto the land. The axolotl skips that last step. It keeps its feathery gills. It keeps its swimming tail. It never leaves the water. Scientists call this staying young forever, and it is very unusual. The axolotl has a second trick that is even stranger. If it loses a leg, it grows a new one. Not a scar, not a stump, but a whole new leg with new bones and new toes. It can do this over and over. Wild axolotls now live in only one place on Earth: a few canals near Mexico City. There are very few left.

blocks.prompt: Forever Young, and Nearly Gone
blocks.text: Almost every salamander lives two lives. The first is spent underwater, breathing through feathery gills. Then comes metamorphosis: the gills shrink, lungs develop, the body reshapes itself, and the animal walks out onto land to begin its second life. The axolotl refuses. It keeps its gills, keeps its paddle tail, and spends every day of its life underwater. Biologists call this neoteny, which means holding on to childhood features forever. The axolotl grows up in every way except its body. Its healing is stranger still. Cut off an axolotl's leg and it does not form a scar. Instead, cells gather at the wound and rebuild the limb from scratch, bone by bone, toe by toe. It can regrow its tail, parts of its spine, and even some of its heart. It can do this dozens of times. Researchers study the axolotl closely, hoping to learn how it heals so completely. Here is the sad part. Wild axolotls survive in one place only: a handful of canals near Mexico City, where the great lake of the Aztecs once spread across the valley. Pollution and hungry introduced fish have taken almost all of them. Thousands live in tanks and laboratories around the world, while the wild population may number in the dozens.

blocks.prompt: The Animal That Refused to Grow Up
blocks.text: Most salamanders live two separate lives. The first is aquatic: the larva hatches with feathery external gills and a broad paddle tail. Then a surge of thyroid hormone triggers metamorphosis. Gills are reabsorbed, lungs develop, the skull reshapes, and the adult hauls itself onto land. The axolotl never receives that signal. It matures, reproduces, and dies still wearing the body of a larva, gills fanned out around its head like a feathered crown. Biologists call the condition neoteny, and the axolotl is its most famous example. Its second peculiarity is more useful and far less understood. Most animals, humans included, answer injury with scar tissue: a fast, cheap patch that seals the wound and stops there. The axolotl answers differently. Cells near the wound reverse their training, forget what they had specialized into, and gather into a blastema, a bud of unfinished cells that rebuilds the missing part from first principles. A leg returns complete with bone, muscle, nerve, and toes, correctly sized and correctly aimed. The axolotl regrows its tail, portions of its spinal cord, its heart, even parts of its eye, and it will do so dozens of times without error. Laboratories worldwide study it for exactly this reason. The irony is bitter. This animal, one of the most studied vertebrates on the planet, is nearly gone from the only place it has ever lived. Wild axolotls persist in a fragment of canals at Xochimilco, near Mexico City, the last damp remainder of the vast lake system the Aztecs built their capital upon. Pollution, urban growth, and introduced carp and tilapia have emptied the water of them. Hundreds of thousands live in tanks; the wild population may be counted in dozens. A creature that can rebuild almost any part of itself cannot rebuild its own lake.

blocks.prompt: Forever Young: The Axolotl's Two Impossible Tricks
blocks.text: The axolotl performs two tricks that should not be possible, and it performs them at the same time. The first is that it never grows up. A typical salamander begins as an aquatic larva with feathery external gills and a paddle tail. In time, a rising tide of thyroid hormone commands metamorphosis: the gills are reabsorbed, lungs mature, the skull remodels, the skin thickens, and the animal steps onto land as a fundamentally different creature. The axolotl's body largely ignores that command. It reaches full sexual maturity while still wearing its larval form, gills fanned around its head like a crown, and it spends its entire life underwater. Biologists call this neoteny. It is not a defect. In the cold, stable, permanent water of its ancestral lakes, there was simply never much reason to leave, and evolution does not build what is not needed. The second trick is regeneration, and it is the reason the axolotl sits in laboratories on every continent. When most vertebrates are injured, they seal the damage with scar tissue. Scarring is fast and cheap, and it is final: the original structure is never restored. The axolotl takes the expensive route. Cells surrounding the wound dedifferentiate, meaning they abandon their specialized identities and revert to a flexible state. They mass into a blastema, and from that unpromising bud a new limb is constructed: bone, cartilage, muscle, blood vessels, nerve, and toes, correctly proportioned and correctly oriented. The animal repeats this dozens of times without accumulating errors. It regrows tail, jaw, portions of the spinal cord, retinal tissue, and sections of its heart. Researchers want to know what instructions the blastema is following, and whether human cells still remember any of them. Here the story turns. The axolotl is among the most intensively studied vertebrates alive and is simultaneously among the most endangered. Its entire natural range is a remnant of canals and floating gardens at Xochimilco, on the southern edge of Mexico City, the last wet trace of the lake system on which the Aztecs founded Tenochtitlan. Sewage, urban expansion, and introduced carp and tilapia have hollowed out that habitat. Surveys once counted thousands of axolotls per square kilometer; recent surveys have struggled to find any. Hundreds of thousands thrive in aquariums and laboratory tanks, genetically narrow and utterly dependent on people. The animal that can rebuild its own heart cannot rebuild its lake, and that limitation is not biological. It is ours.
